actions.justification: MANDATORY: Baseline vital signs assessment is the first step in evaluating any acute presentation. Patient has acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain — continuous monitoring of HR, BP, SpO2, and RR is critical.

MANDATORY: Wells Score is the standard clinical decision tool for PE probability stratification. Pleuritic chest pain and acute dyspnea are classic PE symptoms — Wells Score guides whether D-dimer alone is sufficient or if CTPA is needed.
MANDATORY: D-dimer is the first-line lab test in the PE diagnostic pathway. If Wells Score is low-to-intermediate, a negative D-dimer effectively rules out PE without need for imaging.

12-lead ECG is indicated within 10 minutes per AHA guidelines for acute chest pain to evaluate for STEMI and other arrhythmias. This is a critical initial assessment step for this patient presenting with dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain.
Patient presenting with acute dyspnea; supplemental oxygen is appropriate supportive care during initial assessment to maintain adequate oxygenation, though SpO2 is currently 98%.

Chest X-ray is indicated per AHA acute chest pain guidelines to evaluate alternative diagnoses (pneumothorax, pneumonia, aortic pathology) and is part of the initial assessment for acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain. Also helps in PE workup context.

Echocardiogram can assess for right heart strain, which would support pulmonary embolism diagnosis given the presentation of acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain, and help risk-stratify the patient.

ECG is a critical initial assessment tool for chest pain/dyspnea per AHA guidelines (Class I, LOE B) - evaluates for STEMI, right heart strain patterns (S1Q3T3) consistent with PE, and other arrhythmias. Note: 'order_ecg' is already done but 'order_imaging_ecg' is a distinct available action_id.

Given the presentation of acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain with a completed Wells score assessment and D-dimer ordered, CT pulmonary angiography is the definitive diagnostic test for pulmonary embolism per PE guidelines. This is the next logical step in confirming the working diagnosis.
Pulmonology consultation is appropriate for a patient with acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain to assist with diagnosis and management planning, particularly if PE is confirmed on CT-PA.
Arterial blood gas is indicated to assess oxygenation, ventilation, and acid-base status in a patient with suspected pulmonary embolism presenting with dyspnea.
Lower extremity venous duplex Doppler ultrasound is indicated to evaluate for deep vein thrombosis as a source of suspected pulmonary embolism, per PE workup guidelines.
Echocardiogram is indicated to assess for right ventricular strain or dysfunction, which would guide risk stratification and management in suspected pulmonary embolism.
CBC is warranted to evaluate for infection, anemia, or thrombocytosis that may contribute to or complicate suspected pulmonary embolism presentation with acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain.
BNP helps assess right ventricular strain/dysfunction, which is critical for risk stratification in suspected pulmonary embolism and guides management decisions.
BMP provides baseline renal function (important before contrast imaging and anticoagulation), electrolytes, and metabolic status relevant to this patient's workup.
Troponin is indicated to assess for right heart strain or myocardial injury in the setting of suspected PE with acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain. Not yet ordered per completed actions list.
Coagulation studies (PT/INR/aPTT) are needed prior to anticoagulation therapy to establish baseline and guide dosing in suspected pulmonary embolism.
Serum lactate helps assess tissue perfusion and hemodynamic compromise in suspected PE, aiding risk stratification even with currently stable vitals.

Patient presents with acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain with comprehensive PE workup completed. Hemodynamically stable (HR 80, BP 120/80, SpO2 98%). Per PE management guidelines, anticoagulation should be initiated promptly in suspected/confirmed PE to prevent thrombus extension. Patient is stable so full anticoagulation (not thrombolysis) is appropriate first-line therapy.

LMWH (e.g., enoxaparin) is a guideline-recommended anticoagulant for hemodynamically stable PE. It provides predictable dosing without need for continuous monitoring and is preferred over unfractionated heparin in stable patients without renal failure or high bleeding risk.

Patient presents with acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain, consistent with suspected pulmonary embolism. CT-PA and D-dimer have been ordered, Wells score assessed, and LMWH was given. Transitioning to IV unfractionated heparin (UFH) is appropriate for confirmed or high-suspicion PE, especially if interventional procedures (catheter-directed thrombolysis or embolectomy) may be needed, as UFH is preferred in that setting due to its reversibility and titratable dosing.

Patient with suspected PE (acute dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain) who has received anticoagulation. IV fluid support can help maintain preload in the setting of right heart strain from PE. Vitals are currently stable (HR 80, BP 120/80, SpO2 98%), but IV access and fluid support are appropriate as a precautionary measure while awaiting CT-PA results and further workup.

Patient with acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain has already received anticoagulation and CT-PA has been ordered. Consulting interventional radiology is appropriate for potential catheter-directed therapy or IVC filter placement if PE is confirmed, particularly if the patient deteriorates or has contraindications to thrombolysis. This is a reasonable next step given the workup trajectory.
